children: J.P. Morgan Chase sees a challenging third-quarter earnings season for aerospace and defense companies as slowing airline traffic growth, uncertainty over U.S. military spending and lingering supply-chain constraints weigh on investor sentiment.

In an Oct. 8 research report, Seth M. Seifman, J.P. Morgan's lead aerospace and defense analyst, said most companies should deliver solid quarterly results and express confidence in underlying demand. However, encouraging earnings may not be enough to reverse the sector's recent stock-market weakness.
"The market is near an all-time high but A&D stocks were weak in Q3 and sentiment is sour," Seifman wrote.
The analyst identified Howmet Aerospace
, Honeywell Aerospace
, Huntington Ingalls Industries
and Lockheed Martin
as potential outperformers during earnings season.
J.P. Morgan also downgraded Leidos Holdings
to Neutral from Overweight, citing deteriorating earnings expectations.

For investors, the report highlights a widening divide between aerospace manufacturers benefiting from production growth, defense contractors supported by long-term weapons demand and government services companies facing pressure on revenue and profitability.
Leidos downgraded as earnings outlook weakens
J.P. Morgan reduced its price target on Leidos
to $142 from $160, reflecting concerns about the company's healthcare business and the potential for further earnings disappointments.

The new target still represents about 25% upside from Leidos' Oct. 7 closing price of $113.55. However, Seifman argued that the company's relatively low valuation is insufficient to justify an Overweight rating when other aerospace and defense stocks also offer substantial potential returns.

J.P. Morgan forecasts Leidos' 2027 revenue at approximately $18.1 billion, down from an estimated $18.35 billion in 2026. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization are projected to fall to $2.14 billion from $2.45 billion.

The bank expects the company's adjusted ebitda margin to decline to 11.8% from 13.3%, largely because of weakness in its Health business. Margins in that segment are projected to fall to 16% from 22%.
Seifman noted that Bloomberg consensus estimates still anticipate approximately $2.45 billion in adjusted ebitda for 2027, suggesting that published expectations may be too optimistic.
Leidos

nevertheless has potential growth opportunities in defense products, energy infrastructure and Federal Aviation Administration modernization. A favorable outcome in the Department of Veterans Affairs contract recompete could also improve its outlook.
Howmet and Honeywell offer aerospace opportunities
J.P. Morgan remains constructive on Howmet Aerospace
despite concerns about changes in the aircraft-engine supply chain.
Howmet
shares have faced pressure partly because GE Aerospace

plans to acquire Consolidated Precision Products, while another supplier is developing blade-casting capabilities. These developments have raised questions about Howmet's long-term competitive position in aerospace castings.
Seifman expects Howmet's 2026 earnings estimates to increase and anticipates that management will remain confident about growth in aerospace and industrial gas turbines.

The analyst also sees a potential rebound in Honeywell Aerospace, whose shares have fallen more than 25% since its second-quarter earnings report, compared with a roughly 10% decline in the Industrial Select Sector SPDR Fund
Although Honeywell faces longer-term challenges, JPMorgan believes expectations have fallen sufficiently to limit additional downside, provided the company avoids an earnings miss.
Meanwhile, TransDigm Group

could benefit from a stronger-than-expected initial fiscal 2027 outlook. J.P. Morgan expects aftermarket demand to remain healthy despite concerns about slowing airline traffic and potential changes to aircraft maintenance regulations.

The bank cautioned that stagnant global air traffic could eventually reduce maintenance demand. For now, however, a backlog of engine maintenance work should support aerospace aftermarket suppliers for several more quarters.
Lockheed Martin, Huntington Ingalls favored in defense
J.P. Morgan identified Lockheed Martin
and Huntington Ingalls
as its preferred defense stocks heading into third-quarter results, even though both carry Neutral ratings.
For Lockheed Martin

, the bank expects continued execution improvements and significant backlog growth from missile contracts. Seifman said the company's Missiles and Fire Control business remains an important investment attraction.
Huntington Ingalls
could benefit from progress on major shipbuilding programs, including milestones involving the aircraft carrier John F. Kennedy, designated CVN-79, and a submarine contract awarded in July.
The analyst believes these developments support expectations for profitability and cash flow during the remainder of 2026.
Huntington Ingalls shares have declined approximately 20% since their latest earnings report, compared with declines of 13% for Lockheed Martin and 12% for Northrop Grumman
, potentially creating room for a positive market reaction.
J.P. Morgan remains more cautious on Northrop Grumman
because of its comparatively limited exposure to missile demand and the loss of the Navy's F/A-XX fighter competition.
Midterm elections cloud defense spending outlook
The November congressional elections represent another potential source of volatility for defense contractors.
Defense stocks have been under pressure since March as investors assess whether a change in congressional control could constrain military spending growth.
Seifman suggested that some election-related uncertainty could dissipate after Nov. 3, although negotiations over the fiscal 2027 federal budget may continue well beyond Election Day.
The analyst also flagged rising government borrowing costs as a longer-term consideration, given the potential competition between interest payments and discretionary defense spending.
For investors, the timing of appropriations and contract awards could prove as important as the eventual size of the defense budget.
Boeing retains Overweight rating despite cash flow concerns
J.P. Morgan maintained its Overweight rating on Boeing
and its $290 price target, representing approximately 54% upside from the company's Oct. 7 closing price of $188.32.
The bank continues to see potential for Boeing to improve production of its 737 and 787 aircraft, advance the delayed 777X program and stabilize performance in its defense business.
However, Seifman acknowledged that expectations for Boeing's 2027 cash flow have weakened, while uncertainty about aircraft production rates has contributed to investor caution.

J.P. Morgan forecasts Boeing's revenue rising to $108.46 billion in 2027 from $96.31 billion in 2026. Adjusted free cash flow is projected to increase to approximately $5.55 billion from $1.84 billion.
The bank's longer-term investment thesis depends on Boeing
converting its roughly $500 billion order backlog into aircraft deliveries, stronger cash generation and reduced debt.
J.P. Morgan also maintained its Overweight rating and $40 price target on StandardAero
, citing opportunities in commercial aircraft-engine maintenance and higher-margin component repair services.
Earnings may not be enough to lift sector sentiment
J.P. Morgan's broader message is that aerospace and defense companies face an unusually difficult earnings environment despite generally favorable underlying demand.

Commercial aerospace suppliers continue to benefit from aircraft production requirements and maintenance backlogs, while defense manufacturers have opportunities tied to missiles, shipbuilding and military modernization.
However, elevated expectations for some companies, uncertainty about future government spending and slowing airline traffic growth could limit investors' willingness to pay higher earnings multiples.
Seifman's preferred approach is to focus on companies with opportunities for upward earnings revisions or sufficiently depressed expectations to support a rebound.
That favors Howmet
and Honeywell Aerospace
on the commercial side, alongside Lockheed Martin
and Huntington Ingalls
in defense, while leaving government services providers such as Leidos
facing a more difficult path to recovery.
